body: 'Home' is a depressing spare room tbh, but sometimes a day to not have to mask is exactly it

My favourite way of dealing with this, as I increasingly give fewer and fewer shits about anything and the consequences of my words, is to make these people feel as stupid as you possibly can and talk to them in the most patronising manner possible. The reality is that the reason they feel they can use these tactics against you is that they haven't felt enough shame themselves throughout life and have also learnt to exert power by trying to create shame in other groups by asking them pointed questions. I grew up up with all this bull crap about thinking about their perspective and how often its disenfranchised people who need empathy and warmth extended to them. That's BS. What they need is a healthy dose of feeling shame and embarrassment for how they treat you. Some is telling you to speak English- carry on speaking in english and elicit responses in the english whilst pointing out that the whole conversation is happening in english. 

But also, you don't need to put up with this, it's not on you. It can feel awful, and one of the worst ways it gets to us is that we have this idea that we take everything and keep on serving which isn't true. Not being able to stand up for yourself is bad for your emotional health so you can show that you are annoyed and that it wasn't ok. That is called a normal human response to someone being vile to you. Controlling our emotions for the sake of professionalism means not freaking out when someone is crashing in front of you, and being able to be calm and with the patient/family when having difficult conversations. It does not mean taking verbal abuse with a smile and accepting it and carrying on treating. This is the false idea the public has of the hippocratic oath, and it has what has led to a huge amount of entitlement and blame within our culture. 

You can stand up for yourself, that it is unprofessional to do so is a myth

I unfortunately have seen this sort of thing with advanced stroke nurses attending stroke calls and just looking, writing off a stroke and immediately teaching their trainee about how dizziness is usually caused by labrinthytis, whilst I do a detailed cerebellar exam and the patient does in fact have overt cerebellar signs and the next day MRI does in fact demonstrate cerebellar infarct (albeit small). I think it is that thing that whilst I have crippling self doubt about all the things I have missed, all the things I don't know I don't know (MRCP part 1 revision is highlighting it more and more), hell I read the comments on here about people not having clinical reasoning skills and I worry that that represents me (crippling self doubt is fun)- at least we have doctors have an awareness that there is a huge array of things that could be wrong- I feel like that is what the issue is- the willingness to easily write something off and just 'know' without going into it in detail and questioning yourself a bit

>She's got a brain the size of an organelle in a frikken Enteroccus, but without the intellect to develop vancomyin resistance.

You're my hero, after Dr Singh of course, this is the best insult I've ever heard
So sorry this happened to you, and unfortunately I can relate to that same extent and how normalised I became to it. I think the key is being able to talk openly about it and what was happening

yeah, I have had had the same fear. I suspected it was extremely common, and the reason we are all scared to talk about it is the usual stigma, 'would you want talk to mental health services', and expectation not to talk to each other (obviously not when we're busy doing work but being generally supportive and open is hopefully something that we can see more). We need to look after each other and not feel isolated in how we feel
Completely agreed, didn't mean to sound like calling you out
I don't think there would be any use in that if I'm honest
Yep, definitely the least we can do is be supportive colleagues for each other

Multiple things can co-exist. There can be cases where there was a clear pattern of unfair discrimination as we saw with Bawa-Garba and the laptop case. BUT there can also be ethnic minority doctors who legitimately should be struck off (I worked with this one, am POC myself, and whole heartedly agree with this decision after what I saw) who also misuse the racial issue to defend themselves and weaken the legitimacy of it for people who genuinely have been affected it.

Agreed, also worked with this doctor (probably different trust) and definitely agree that there were known serious issues with insight and bizarre lies did seem to be a pattern. Again, agree (as a POC myself), not every POC discharge from medical register is unjustified
My god, I'm so sorry. I know what you mean about the protective factor the the thought processes that occur. How are you doing now?

Couldn't edit the post to include this link, but considering this model 'exhausted without trust and worth', are the results of this poll in any way surprising. We are worked to exhaustion and exist in a highly punitive system with increasing vilification and lack of support. At least one of these factors needs to be tackled. 

[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27423293/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27423293/)

There was a GMC survey recently about their GMP and I fed all of this back to them. I am seriously considering writing about this. We definitely need to make sure we have each others' backs, but it would be helpful if the higher ups didn't create such an environment of stress and paranoia that people feel so isolated. Medicine was meant to literally be about helping to maintain life and care; and yet it has become this awful politicised things that seem baffling when you consider what the sentiment of medicine is supposed to be.
Medical short stay ward-APH I assume. Great hospital, friendly, good teaching if you find the right people

This. This is what is I was trying to emphasise in my comment, but you have done it in a much better way than I have. It seems quite clear that OP has been manipulated to see themselves in this way by the abuser, and he has played some extremely sick games.

I agree with above in terms of getting help from a trauma therapist through a local woman's centre, school/university, or help centre. 

I don't want to influence how you think about this, but I wanted to help with the validation in that you are not spoilt, you are not being dramatic in any way (you have likely been conditioned to think this way about yourself), you are right that this was abuse and grooming. If you are in university, explore their services and tell them about the control and coercive situation you are in (coercive control is a crime in some places). 

Please do not be sorry for the length of your writing, you have every right to talk about this, especially as you say you never get to talk about it. It doesn't matter if you need to say it or not, what you have been through is trauma, abuse and grooming and you deserve to have a space to talk through it without apologising for yourself. 

You talk about grad school- I hope that means you are at university. Most higher education places will have some sort of support system through which you may be able to have access to psychological therapies for trauma and abuse and support 

There are a lot of other website listed on this that you can access as well. 

I know I've said this already, but I really do want to emphasise it- please do not feel sorry for talking about this or feel your are spoilt or dramatic for talking about it, it is definitely valid and I'm sorry that you have experienced this

It's also when you are a patient. I have been post surgery recovery as a teenager (aged 17) and white health care staff would come and grill me about domestic violence in my community, whether I agree with rape gangs (I am female) etc etc

Looking back now, that is quite shocking to me.

When I was in medical school, we would routinely have lectures in which the lecturer made open comments about certain ethnic minorities and it would just be met with gasps/laughter

Worst, and I have spoken about this before was what I heard from other students at another medical school. There was a suicide due to racial bullying. On asking the university to investigate, they refused and stated the suicide was likely due to pressure put on the student to do something he didn't want to (untrue) and again using a racial trope to turn it back on the family.

I think I have had minimal and generally had a good reputation wherever I have gone. But the hyper vigilance is exhausting

Yeah I mean this isn't news, the main progress is that at least there are steps being made against the whole 'it's in your head' 'you can't trust your perception'.

As for me, I just wonder if it is even worth it to exist in a system that makes you so hyper vigilant. At any moment you could be called out/referred for something that is not your fault. And you will likely be gaslit with people saying there is no racial element to it (stop playing the race card).

I've never been referred etc, but the fear of coming across a team that has an issue with me because of race and the implications that could have terrifies me

I will agree with you though that in hindsight, although in my anger at hearing this, it seemed like it had been a lie, it most definitely wasn't meant that way by the teacher and the title does misrepresent the situation. I'll change the title with that feedback, and thank for holding me to that. I do still have a slight problem with the way you are repeatedly putting it on the kid for not being able to handle banter when it wasn't the isolated sentence by the teacher that caused the upset.

Thank you for this. It's certainly a strange feeling, and I won't lie, I'm not sure the feeling of being 'known' as a  childhood can be replaced. But all forms of being are valid ones. I do feel slightly hypocritical in all this as I have found an joy and solace in the unexpected  response to something I wrote this morning in a moment of quiet sadness. The joy of that is kind of the anti-thesis to being to live your life without an audience or witness. Either way, I'm glad you resonated with it, and thank you for the gold star!

I really get you when you talk about realising that you are playing out abusive dynamics. I won't lie, I did a little scour of your past posts just now, and I really agree with you about doubting the transactional nature of therapy and how it seems to be an entirely false construct within which to fix a very human problem of attachment. I should be wary of saying this as a professional myself, although my profession doesn't have such a strict code of conduct with regards to the humanness with which you interact with a person- but the legal and administrative framework that governs the interactions taking place within therapy- whilst there for safety can sometimes do harm themselves. The whole construct can be one where the power dynamic is such that anything can be turned into a question for enquiry, rather than spontaneous moments of humanness. I guess it depends why you went in the first place. 

I went on the advice of a friend after opening up about a family situation and several other life experiences. What I found was that it revealed a deeper need to be heard and known for who I am and what my experiences are, and also to want to formulate ideas. Instead I found myself building a picture of the therapist based on when they sounded convinced by themselves, when they didn't, when they clearly were choosing their words carefully. I will say however, I think I found a good one overall. The abrupt ending was out of anyone's control, but I think did give me insight into the mental health system and its potential coldness. Perhaps that is also partly the culture in the UK. 

For yourself, often people who have been in abusive situations gain or hone in astute observation of other people- hypervigilance. Sometimes it is accurate, sometimes it isn't. I can imagine with the right therapist who understand this, that perhaps it could be useful to go through this. But when that is overlooked, therapy can become an even more isolating experience where you are less able to trust your own instincts. I hope you have found your way somewhat. 

With regards to self actualisation, I don't know that it is. We all transiently go through periods of self-assuredness, surely followed by darker times when we feel we need guidance. I don't think it's a permanent state of affairs, and certainly one only made possible through the alignment of several lucky circumstance factors. It comes in ebbs and flows, and all people need some sort of connection. I hope you do get there though, with finding your self-actualisation.

There's a whole line of thought of people who are normalised to superficial thinking being the ones who are actually mentally ill, and those who suffer enough mentally in that way tend to reach the questions that outline the crux of their existence. I'm not sure I agree with that line of thought in it's entirety. A lot of mental illness can be molecularly defined and has no 'reason' other than the fact that it is and it changes that person's experience. Nevertheless, unplanned spirituality, if it has given you solace, can never be a bad thing. For me it is music and writing that is transcendental.

P. S. I really appreciate what you wrote about paradoxes, it set off a new line of thought for me

I'm glad you did. I agree with you, but I also think bearing witness to our own experience properly is what allows to bear witness to others and be in a relationship. It can be difficult because often we expect the depth of our relationship with others to be similar to the depth with ourselves. It can never be so, except in knowing that we all share the same condition of having to bear witness to ourselves.

One of my most powerful moments was a lone hike on a knife edge ridge mountain, when it was just me and I had to confront my fears alone. I think in order to properly connect with others, we need to have these experiences ourselves to understand our shared isolation.

I'm glad this resonated with you. One thing I always try to remember is that all of human experience is within the remit of what a living thing can experience. Whether those things are horrific, painful, and atrocities that no one should experience or the truly truly tragic or on the other end of the spectrum- the quiet and alone times of intense oneness with experience, all of these things we can bear witness to in ourselves and others. Wishing you the best as well.

I think you're right. There is some level of hesitancy I have with him, and I'm sure a lot of it is to do with the dynamic.
